intro:
# Why defending is hard

Seeing your opponent's tactic is harder than seeing your own. You first have to picture your own move, then look at the board from the other side, and pick out the most dangerous of several threats. Most tactics training is also done from the attacking side.

Even grandmasters miss it. In Rogers-Kortchnoi, Biel 1986, Black is in check, and two king moves keep the queen protected. [1...Ke5] was safe, since White can only repeat checks with [1...Ke5 2.Qg5+ Kd6]. Kortchnoi played 1...Kc5?? and was mated by 2.Qc7#.

This deck teaches six ways to defend your king and six ways to defend your other pieces. Each comes with a short page, a card that asks you to describe it, and two puzzles.

chapters.name: Picking the right square
intro:
# Picking the right square

When your king is in check and has more than one square, don't take the first one that looks safe. Go through every king move, find the opponent's strongest reply to each, and pick the square where no mate follows.

Black is in check and has three squares. Two of them walk into mate: [1...Kg5 2.Qf4#] and [1...Ke5 2.Qe7#]. On e6 the king always keeps a free square, so White can only keep checking, and the game ends in a repetition.

cards.front: Your king is in danger. Describe the defence "picking the right square".

back.text:
Your king is in check: try every square it can go to, look for the opponent's best reply to each, and choose the one that does not lead to mate.

Here [1...Kg5 2.Qf4#] and [1...Ke5 2.Qe7#] lose; on e6 White has only checks.

front.text: You are in check. Defend by picking the right square for the king.

back.text: Only the h5-square is safe. The other two lose to the same queen move: [1.Kf4 Qe5#]; [1.Kf5 Qe5#].

front.text: You are in check. Defend.

back.text: 1...Kh6, after which White has no more than checks. g4 looks just as good but is mate: [1...Kg4 2.Qe2#].

chapters.name: Trading the attacker
intro:
# Trading the attacker

When mate is threatened but you are not in check, you have one free move to stop it. The cleanest way is to trade off the piece that makes the threat: once it is gone, so is the threat.
White threatens 2.Qg7#. Black offers the queen trade with check, and after 1...Qe6+ 2.Qxe6 fxe6 the mate is gone and Black's a-pawn decides the game.

cards.front: Your king is in danger. Describe the defence "trading the attacker".

back.text:
Mate is threatened: trade off the piece that threatens it.

Here White threatens 2.Qg7#, and 1...Qe6+ forces the queens off.

front.text: Mate is threatened. Defend by trading the attacker.

back.text: 1...Ng4+ trades off the e5-knight, which threatened 2.Ng6#. Covering g6 is not enough: [1...Be4 2.Nf7#].

front.text: Mate is threatened. Defend.

back.text: 1...Qb1+ forces the queens off, and Black wins the knight ending. Guarding g8 with the queen still loses: [1...Qg7 2.Qe8+ Qg8 3.Qxg8#].

chapters.name: Pinning the attacker
intro:
# Pinning the attacker

A pinned piece can't make its threat. So if the attacker can't be traded, look for a way to pin it to the king or to a bigger piece.
Black threatens 1...g4#. 1.Rb5 pins the g5-pawn to the black king on h5, so it can't move, and White is out of danger.

cards.front: Your king is in danger. Describe the defence "pinning the attacker".

back.text:
Mate is threatened: pin the piece that threatens it, so it can't make the mating move.

Here Black threatens 1...g4#, and 1.Rb5 pins the pawn to the black king.

front.text: Mate is threatened. Defend by pinning the attacker.

back.text: White threatens 2.Qg7#. 1...Qd8 pins the white queen to the king on h4; the best White has is 2.Qxd8 Nxd8, with a level ending.

front.text: Mate is threatened. Defend.

back.text: 1.Rf5 pins the d5-pawn to the black king, which stops [1.f7 d4#]. Then the f-pawn wins the game for White.

chapters.name: Blocking a line
intro:
# Blocking a line

A long-range piece helps with the mate along a file, rank or diagonal. Put one of your pieces on that line, and it no longer reaches the square that matters.
Black threatens 1...Rg1#: the rook would be backed up by the bishop on a7. 1.Bd4 stands on the a7-g1 diagonal, so the rook on g1 would no longer be protected.

cards.front: Your king is in danger. Describe the defence "blocking a line".

back.text:
Mate is threatened: put a piece on the file, rank or diagonal that one of the attackers works along, so it no longer helps with the mate.

Here 1.Bd4 cuts the a7-bishop off from g1, where Black threatened to mate with the rook.

front.text: Mate is threatened. Defend by blocking a line.

back.text: 1...Rg5 cuts the h5-rook off from the fifth rank and gives the king its squares back. Otherwise [1...Bf8 2.b3#], or [1...f2 2.Rc5#].

front.text: Mate is threatened. Defend.

back.text: Black threatens 1...Bg3#, with the d8-rook keeping the king off the d-file. 1.Rd7 blocks the file and attacks that rook at the same time.

chapters.name: Defending the critical square
intro:
# Defending the critical square

Find the square the mate would be given on, and cover it with one of your pieces. If the opponent can't land there, there is no mate.
Black threatens 1...Nc1#. 1.Bg5 covers c1 from a distance, and the knight can't go there.

cards.front: Your king is in danger. Describe the defence "defending the critical square".

back.text:
Mate is threatened: find the square the mate would be given on, and cover it.

Here Black threatens 1...Nc1#, and 1.Bg5 covers c1.

front.text: Mate is threatened. Defend the critical square.

back.text: Black threatens 1...Nf3#. 1.Ng1 covers f3. Taking the f4-pawn doesn't help, since the mate is still there: [1.Nxf4 gxf4 2.a7 Nf3#].

front.text: Mate is threatened. Defend.

back.text: White threatens 2.Rf5#. 1...Rf8 covers f5, and the game is level.

chapters.name: Creating an escape square
intro:
# Creating an escape square

A check is only mate when the king has nowhere to go. Move a pawn or piece off a square next to your king, and the mating check becomes an ordinary one.
Black threatens 1...Ne5#: every square around the white king is covered or taken. 1.f4 clears f3, so after a knight check the king can step there.

cards.front: Your king is in danger. Describe the defence "creating an escape square".

back.text:
Mate is threatened: move a pawn or piece off a square next to your king, so the king has somewhere to go when the check comes.

Here Black threatens 1...Ne5#, and 1.f4 frees f3 for the king.

front.text: Mate is threatened. Defend by creating an escape square.

back.text: White threatens 2.Re8#. 1...b6 frees b7 for the king. In the game Black took a pawn and was mated: [1...Rxh2 2.Re8#].

front.text: Mate is threatened. Defend.

back.text: Black threatens 1...Bh3#. 1.g6 frees g5 for the king, and the bishop check is no longer mate. Anything else allows it: [1.b6 Bh3#].

chapters.name: Picking the right square
intro:
# Picking the right square

The usual way to save an attacked piece is to move it. But before you do, check each square it could go to for a tactic the opponent has against it there.

The bishop attacks the c7-knight, and nothing can protect it. The two squares worth a look are a6, where it takes a pawn on the edge of the board, and d5 in the centre. d5 loses the knight to a discovered attack: [1.Nd5 Bg3 2.Rb1 Rxd5]. After 1.Nxa6 Ra8 2.Nb4 the knight is safe.

cards.front: One of your pieces is in danger. Describe the defence "picking the right square".

back.text:
Move the attacked piece, but first check every square it can go to for a tactic against it.

Here the knight goes to a6 and back to b4; on d5 it would be lost to a discovered attack.

front.text: One of your pieces is in danger. Defend by picking the right square for it.

back.text: 1.Ng6 is safe. On f3 the knight runs into a discovered check from the b8-bishop: [1.Nf3 e4+ 2.g3 exf3].

front.text: One of your pieces is in danger. Defend.

back.text: 1.Rd3. On e6 the rook runs out of squares, and in the game it was lost: [1.Re6 Kf7 2.Re3 Nxe3].

chapters.name: Trading the attacker
intro:
# Trading the attacker

When a piece is attacked and can't be saved by moving it, find the piece that does the most damage and trade it off.
The a2-rook pins the d2-bishop to the white king, and nothing can protect the bishop. 1.Ra5+ forces the rooks off: after 1...Rxa5 2.Bxa5 the bishop is free and White is two pawns up.

cards.front: One of your pieces is in danger. Describe the defence "trading the attacker".

back.text:
Trade off the piece that attacks yours.

Here the a2-rook pins the d2-bishop, and 1.Ra5+ forces it to be traded.

front.text: One of your pieces is in danger. Defend by trading the attacker.

back.text: The b2-rook pins the knight to the king and attacks it. 1...Rd2+ forces 2.Rxd2 Nxd2, and the knight is free.

front.text: One of your pieces is in danger. Defend.

back.text: The d6-bishop pins the queen to the king. 1...Bc5+ gives check and forces that bishop to be traded: 2.Bxc5 Qxc5+.

chapters.name: Pinning the attacker
intro:
# Pinning the attacker

Pin the piece that attacks yours, so that carrying out its threat costs the opponent something.
The f6-pawn attacks both white rooks. 1.Re6 attacks the pawn with the h6-rook behind it: if it takes on g5, White takes the h6-rook, and after 1...fxg5 2.Rxh6 material is level.

cards.front: One of your pieces is in danger. Describe the defence "pinning the attacker".

back.text:
Pin the piece that attacks yours, so that it can't take without losing something itself.

Here 1.Re6 pins the f6-pawn to the h6-rook.

front.text: One of your pieces is in danger. Defend by pinning the attacker.

back.text: 1.Rb5 pins the f5-rook to the black king, so it can't take the queen. Every other move loses the queen.

front.text: One of your pieces is in danger. Defend.

back.text: The e4-pawn forks both rooks. 1.Rd4 pins it to the h4-rook: after 1...exf3 2.Rxh4 material is level.

chapters.name: Defending the critical square
intro:
# Defending the critical square

Sometimes the danger is a square, not a piece: one jump or move there would attack several of your pieces at once. Cover that square before the opponent gets there.

From d4 the knight would attack the king, the b3-rook and the c6-bishop at once. Moving one of them leaves another to be taken: [1.Rb2 Nd4+ 2.Ke3 Nxc6]. 1.Ke3 covers d4. 1.Ke4 covers it as well, but runs into a different fork: [1.Ke4 Nc5+ 2.Ke3 Nxb3].

cards.front: One of your pieces is in danger. Describe the defence "defending the critical square".

back.text:
Find the square from which the opponent would win material, often with a fork, and cover it.

Here 1.Ke3 covers d4, where the knight would fork king, rook and bishop.

front.text: One of your pieces is in danger. Defend the critical square.

back.text: The b2-rook has to keep covering c3, where the bishop would attack it and threaten ...Be1# at the same time. 1.Rb3 does that; on b4 it doesn't: [1.Rb4 Bc3 2.Bg4 Bxb4].

front.text: One of your pieces is in danger. Defend.

back.text: Once the bishop leaves the e-file, ...Re1# is threatened, so it has to reach f2 to cover e1. 1.Bc5+ b6 2.Bf2 gets it there with a check on the way. [1.Bg5 Re1#].

chapters.name: Protecting the piece
intro:
# Protecting the piece

A king can't be protected, but any other piece can. If the attacked piece can't move, bring another piece to defend it, with a check on the way if it needs time to get there.
The g8-bishop pins the d5-knight to the king on a2. 1.Bf5+ gains a move with check, and after 1...Kh6 2.Be4 the knight is protected.

cards.front: One of your pieces is in danger. Describe the defence "protecting the piece".

back.text:
When the attacked piece can't move away, defend it with another piece.

Here 1.Bf5+ Kh6 2.Be4 brings the bishop to the pinned knight with a check on the way.

front.text: One of your pieces is in danger. Defend by protecting it.

back.text: 1...Re5 protects the knight and frees e7 for the king, which also stops [1...Nd6 2.Rh8#].

front.text: One of your pieces is in danger. Defend.

back.text: The g8-rook attacks the pinned g2-bishop, and the d5-bishop attacks the b7-rook. 1.Rb2 saves the rook and protects the bishop along the second rank.

chapters.name: The counterattack
intro:
# The counterattack

Instead of moving or protecting the attacked piece, attack something of the opponent's. If they have to answer your threat, you get the move you need to save your own piece.

The c6-pawn attacks the d5-knight, and the knight has no safe square. 1.f5 attacks the g6-knight and frees f4 at the same time. After 1...Ne5 2.Nf4 the knight is safe; [1...cxd5 2.fxg6] only trades knights.

cards.front: One of your pieces is in danger. Describe the defence "the counterattack".

back.text:
Attack one of the opponent's pieces instead, to win the move you need to save your own.

Here 1.f5 attacks the g6-knight and frees f4 for the d5-knight.

front.text: One of your pieces is in danger. Defend with a counterattack.

back.text: 1.Rb1 attacks the b5-bishop, which is pinned to the king. After 1...c6 White has time for 2.Bc4. Running away at once allows mate: [1.Bh5 Rf1#].

front.text: One of your pieces is in danger. Defend.

back.text: The c4-pawn forks both rooks. 1...Rf5 attacks the f2-rook, and after 2.Rxf5 Rxf5 the fork is gone.

cards.front: Which six ways to defend your king are in this deck?
cards.back:
1. Picking the right square
2. Trading the attacker
3. Pinning the attacker
4. Blocking a line
5. Defending the critical square
6. Creating an escape square

cards.front: Which six ways to defend one of your pieces are in this deck?
cards.back:
1. Picking the right square
2. Trading the attacker
3. Pinning the attacker
4. Defending the critical square
5. Protecting the piece
6. The counterattack

cards.front: Which four defences work both for your king and for your pieces?
cards.back:
1. Picking the right square
2. Trading the attacker
3. Pinning the attacker
4. Defending the critical square

cards.front: Which two defences are only taught for the king?
cards.back:
Blocking a line and creating an escape square.

C: an escape square only matters against mate. Blocking a line works for pieces too; the book just doesn't list it there.

cards.front: Which two defences are only taught for pieces, and why don't they save a king?
cards.back:
Protecting the piece and the counterattack.

A king can't be protected: when it is attacked it must get out of check. C: a counterattack is too slow against mate unless it is a check; the book gives no reason.
